learn.hook: What happens when an old animal story learns to rhyme? It becomes a fable in verse!
points: 'The Raven and the Fox' is a fable told as a poem: a clever fox tricks a bird by praising it.
A fable is a short story, often with animals that talk, which teaches a moral (a lesson).
'In verse' means written in lines of poetry, often with rhythm and rhyme, instead of ordinary paragraphs (prose).
A group of lines in a poem is called a stanza. Words that end with the same sound, like 'tight' and 'delight', are rhyming words.
Many famous fables come from Aesop (ancient Greece) and from the Panchatantra (ancient India).

example.q: Read this original poem: A myna sat upon a tree, / A roti in her beak held tight. / A jackal called, "O bird so fair, / Your song must be a pure delight!" / She sang out loud — the roti fell; / He grabbed it quick and ran from sight. / Now Myna knows that honeyed words / Can hide a plan that isn't right. Which words rhyme, and what is the moral?
steps: Look at the last word of each line: tree, tight, fair, delight, fell, sight, words, right.
'tight', 'delight', 'sight' and 'right' all end with the same '-ight' sound.
The myna lost her roti because she believed the jackal's sweet words.
So the lesson is about not trusting flattery.
example.answer: Rhyming words: tight, delight, sight, right. Moral: don't be fooled by sweet words of flattery.

learn.reallife: Panchatantra tales, Jataka tales and cartoon fables on TV all teach a moral through animal characters.

quiz.q: What is a fable?
options: A true report about a famous person
A long poem about the sea
A short story, often with talking animals, that teaches a moral
quiz.explain: Fables are short stories, usually with animal characters, that end with a lesson.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a fable with a biography or a report

quiz.q: 'The Raven and the Fox' is a fable 'in verse'. What does 'in verse' mean?
quiz.explain: Verse means poetry: lines with rhythm, often with rhyme.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the difference between verse and prose

quiz.q: In the poem, which word rhymes with 'tight'?
quiz.explain: 'Tight' and 'delight' both end with the '-ight' sound.
quiz.mistake: Looks at spelling or meaning instead of the ending sound

quiz.q: In the poem, the jackal said, "O bird so fair, your song must be a pure delight!" Why did he say this?
options: To make the myna open her beak and drop the roti
To make friends with the myna
quiz.explain: He wanted the roti, so he praised her to make her sing and drop it.
quiz.mistake: Believes the jackal's words were honest praise

quiz.q: In the poem, what happened when the myna sang out loud?
options: She flew away with the roti
The roti fell and the jackal grabbed it
quiz.explain: Opening her beak to sing made the roti fall, and the jackal ran off with it.
quiz.mistake: Does not follow the sequence of events in the poem

quiz.q: What is the moral of the myna-and-jackal poem?
options: Do not be fooled by sweet words of flattery
quiz.explain: The myna lost her food because she trusted the jackal's honeyed words.
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail of the story instead of its lesson

quiz.q: A group of lines in a poem is called a:
quiz.explain: Poems are divided into stanzas, just as prose is divided into paragraphs.
quiz.mistake: Uses the prose word 'paragraph' for poetry

quiz.q: Which ancient Indian collection is famous for animal fables?
quiz.explain: The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of animal fables with morals.
quiz.mistake: Does not know any traditional source of fables

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My teacher says this poem is a fable in verse. What is a fable, and what does in verse mean?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! A fable is a lesson-story, and verse means it's a poem. Rhyme time!
teach.nudge: And what do we learn at the end of a fable?

topics.title: Flattery: sweet words with a hidden plan

learn.hook: If someone suddenly says you're the best singer in the whole universe, should you smile — or check your tiffin?
points: Flattery is praise that is too much and not sincere, usually given to get something from the person.
Honest praise is true and fair: 'Your drawing has lovely colours.' Flattery is over the top: 'You are the greatest artist who ever lived!'
Word family: flatter (verb), flattery (noun), flatterer (a person who flatters).
'Honeyed words' and 'sweet talk' are phrases for pleasant words that may hide a trick. The idiom 'to butter someone up' (in Hindi, 'makkhan lagana') means to flatter them.
A wise person enjoys kind words but still thinks: 'Is this true? Why is this person saying it?'

example.q: Think it through: Raju tells Aman, 'You're the smartest boy in the whole world! Can I copy your homework?' Is this honest praise or flattery?
steps: The praise is far too big to be true.
Raju wants something right after praising: to copy homework.
Too-big praise + a hidden purpose = flattery.
example.answer: It is flattery, because the praise is exaggerated and is used to get something.

learn.reallife: Advertisements and some online messages flatter you ('Lucky winner! You are special!') to make you click or buy — so think before you trust.

games.title: Honest praise or flattery?
items: Your essay had a strong ending.
You are the cleverest person on Earth, lend me ₹50!
Nobody in history has ever sung like you!
Thanks for helping me with the maths sum.
You're a genius, now give me your chocolate.

items.text: The fox tried to ___ the raven.
She felt ___ by his kind words.

quiz.q: What is flattery?
options: Too much praise, often not sincere, given to get something
quiz.explain: Flattery is exaggerated praise with a hidden purpose.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all praise is flattery

quiz.q: Which sentence is honest praise?
options: You are the greatest player the universe has ever seen!
Nobody can ever be as wonderful as you, so give me your bat.
You batted well in today's match.
You are a superstar, now do my homework.
quiz.explain: It is true, fair and asks for nothing in return.
quiz.mistake: Cannot tell fair praise from exaggerated praise

quiz.q: A person who flatters others is called a:
quiz.explain: Adding -er to the verb 'flatter' gives the person who does it: flatterer.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the noun for the act with the noun for the person

quiz.q: In the poem, the myna learns that "honeyed words can hide a plan that isn't right." 'Honeyed words' means:
quiz.explain: Honey is sweet, so 'honeyed words' are sweet-sounding words.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally

quiz.q: 'Stop buttering me up!' What does 'buttering up' mean here?
quiz.explain: To butter someone up is an idiom meaning to flatter them to get something.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: What is the best thing to do when someone flatters you?
options: Give them whatever they ask for
Enjoy kind words but think about why they are said
quiz.explain: A wise person stays polite but thinks about the purpose behind the praise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks flattery must be either believed fully or met with anger

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'sincere'?
quiz.explain: The opposite of 'sincere' is 'insincere', formed with the prefix 'in-'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'un-' or 'dis-' without checking the real word

quiz.q: Why do flatterers praise people too much?
options: To help others improve their work
quiz.explain: Flatterers use praise as a tool to get something, like the jackal and the roti.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the hidden purpose behind flattery

teach.ask: Gappu is excited: 'Someone told me I'm the most beautiful bird in the galaxy! Then he asked for my seeds. What just happened?'
teach.praise: Tweet! That was flattery — too-sweet praise used as a trick. My seeds are staying with me!
teach.nudge: But why do you think he praised me so much just before asking for my seeds?

learn.hook: The jackal didn't just say 'nice bird' — he piled on adjectives! Let's learn how to compare with them.
points: An adjective describes a noun: a clever jackal, a hungry myna, a tall tree.
Adjectives have three degrees: positive (sweet), comparative (sweeter) and superlative (sweetest).
Use the comparative (+ 'than') for two things: 'The fox is cleverer than the raven.' Use the superlative (+ 'the') for three or more: 'the tallest tree'.
Short adjectives add -er/-est (tall, taller, tallest); long ones use more/most (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful).
Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; many, more, most.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in: 'Of all the birds in the garden, the peacock is the ___ (colourful).'
steps: 'Of all the birds' compares more than two, so we need the superlative.
'Colourful' is a long adjective, so it uses 'most'.

learn.reallife: Shopping and sports talk is full of comparisons: 'This mango is sweeter', 'Rohit is the fastest runner in our class.'

items.text: An elephant is ___ than a horse.
Mount Everest is the ___ mountain in the world.
This poem is ___ than that story.
My cold is ___ today than yesterday.
Of the three sisters, Asha is the ___.

quiz.q: Which word is an adjective in: 'The hungry myna sat on a branch'?
quiz.explain: 'Hungry' describes the myna, so it is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the noun or verb with the describing word

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happier.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change y to i

quiz.q: What is the superlative degree of 'good'?
quiz.explain: 'Good' is irregular: good, better, best.
quiz.mistake: Treats an irregular adjective as regular

quiz.q: Which comparison of two people is correct?
options: Rani is taller than her brother.
Rani is tallest than her brother.
Rani is more taller than her brother.
Rani is tall than her brother.
quiz.explain: Comparing two people needs the comparative form 'taller' with 'than'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the superlative or a double comparative for two things

quiz.q: Fill in: 'The Ganga is one of the ___ rivers in India.'
quiz.explain: 'One of the ...' is followed by a superlative: one of the longest rivers.
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative after 'one of the'

quiz.q: What is the comparative of 'beautiful'?
quiz.explain: Long adjectives use 'more' for the comparative.
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to a long adjective

quiz.q: What is the comparative of 'bad'?
quiz.explain: 'Bad' is irregular: bad, worse, worst.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up worse (comparative) and worst (superlative)

quiz.q: What is the superlative of 'big'?
quiz.explain: Short adjectives ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: big → biggest.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the final consonant

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I say my nest is better than my cousin's and the best in the whole tree?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Better for two, best for all. My nest is the cosiest!
teach.nudge: And when I compare my nest with ALL the nests in the tree, which form do I use?
